I'd probably use DP for this.

DP (dynamic programming) is basically a smarter way of brute-forcing something than a naive recursive depth-first search. It trades memory for speed by storing a table of previous subproblem results to quickly reference instead of recalculating recursively each time.

So here, my subproblem is how to incorporate the next digit. I can choose between starting a new term which is added, starting a new term which is multiplied, or concatenating it to the previous term. So I simply make a list of all possible solutions with just the first digit (there is 1), then I incorporate the next digit, so I have 3 possible solutions. Then the next, and so forth. If 2 solutions have the same value and the last term and operation are the same, I can get rid of one of them to save memory, but that probably won't happen often.

So for the string "1122" I get

{"1"}

then

{"11", "1+1", 1*1"}

then

{"112", "11+2", "11*2", "1+12", "1+1+2", "1+1*2", "1*12", "1*1+2", "1*1*2"}

and so forth. At the end I just look through my list to see if any match the target. If there are no 0s later than my position in the string I can delete any potential solutions with a greater value than my target. The worst-case performance is O(3^n) so this would fail for very large inputs, but for your examples it would function. I don't know any non-brute force way to handle this.
